context_blurb:
Your body makes billions of new cells every day: red blood cells in the bone marrow, a fresh gut lining every few days, new cells to close a cut. Each comes from an older cell dividing in two, in a fixed order called the cell cycle. When that order fails, the result can be cancer.

Walther Flemming named mitosis, the division of a cell's nucleus, in 1882 for the threads that appear as a nucleus divides: chromosomes, strands of DNA carrying the genes. He took interphase, the time between divisions, for a rest. It is not: Alma Howard and Stephen Pelc fed bean root tips radioactive phosphorus, which goes into new DNA. The label entered the nuclei in one part of interphase, before any threads showed, so a cell copies its DNA in interphase, before mitosis begins. They named that part the S phase, for synthesis.

In prophase the chromosomes coil up thick; in metaphase they line up across the cell's middle. Each is now two identical copies, and spindle fibres from the cell's two ends, or poles, grip one copy each. The cell waits until every chromosome is gripped from both sides, which guards against a new cell getting both copies of a chromosome when, in anaphase, the copies are pulled to opposite poles. Moving on too soon can leave one cell with an extra chromosome, an error common in tumour cells.

Then cytokinesis splits the cell itself. An animal cell is squeezed in two by a tightening ring of protein fibres, but a plant cell's wall is too stiff, and its water pressure pushes back. So a plant cell builds a new wall from the centre outward: sacs from the Golgi apparatus fuse into a cell plate that spreads until it meets the old wall.

Mitosis grows the body, mends wounds and replaces worn cells. The hair roots, the gut lining and the bone marrow, which replaces red cells that last about four months, never stop dividing. Many chemotherapy drugs fight cancer by stopping cell division, so they also strike these healthy tissues, whose cells divide again and again.

A body's trillions of cells all descend from one first cell, yet nerve cells carry signals and muscle cells pull on bone. Nearly every cell keeps the full set of genes, but each kind puts a different set of its genes to work, steered by signals around it. August Weismann proposed that specialising cells lose hereditary material; John Gurdon's frogs showed they keep it.

In 1962 Gurdon wrecked a frog egg's nucleus with ultraviolet light and gave it a nucleus from a gut cell of a feeding tadpole; a few eggs became tadpoles. The donor nuclei had a mutation leaving one nucleolus, a small dark body in the nucleus, instead of the normal two. The new tadpoles' single nucleolus settled the doubt that the egg's own nucleus, surviving the light, had built the tadpole. A Basel team later did it with a white blood cell's nucleus.

In 2006 Kazutoshi Takahashi and Shinya Yamanaka put two dozen genes, all active in stem cells that can become any cell type, into fibroblasts, mouse connective-tissue cells, resetting a very few. Leaving out one gene at a time showed that four were each needed. To show they were enough, the two put in the four alone, with none of the other twenty, and those four reset cells by themselves.

Leland Hartwell and Ted Weinert broke the DNA of baker's yeast with X-rays. Normal cells paused before dividing; yeast cells whose RAD9 gene was broken kept dividing and soon died. Held still by a drug that blocks division, those cells mended their DNA. So RAD9 does not mend DNA; its job is making the cell wait until the damage is mended. Hartwell called such controls checkpoints. He shared the 2001 Nobel Prize with Paul Nurse, who found the enzyme, a protein that speeds a chemical change, that drives a cell through its cycle, and Tim Hunt, who found cyclins, proteins that build up through each cycle and are destroyed at every division.

Cancer is cell division that no longer stops when it should. In a dish, healthy cells divide until they cover it one cell deep, then stop with food to spare. Cancer cells usually lose that check: they go on dividing, and pile up over one another. Many also divide fast, but their mark is that they do not stop. In the body the pile becomes a tumour.
